web_blocks.html: What JPMorgan Chase Does & Updated Audit Findings: JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE: JPM) is America's top universal bank [1]. In FY2025, it generated $182.45 billion in GAAP net revenue and $57.05 billion in net income [1]. In 9M 2026, revenue rose 15% YoY to $157.36 billion while net income reached $52.95 billion [28]. Q3 2026 ROTCE hit 20% reported (21% adjusted) on 14.0% CET1 capital ($304.15 billion) [28, 35]. Asset & Wealth Management expanded to $5.21 trillion in AUM ($7.90 trillion client assets at 45% ROE) [28]. Still, our Pass 1 blind audit found real capital and cost drags [28]. Q3 AOCI losses widened -$12.13 billion to -$19.82 billion, pulling TBVPS down from $113.35 to $112.64 [28]. Unrecorded HTM bond losses reached $25.84 billion (-$7.38/sh after tax, trimming economic TBVPS to $105.26), and buybacks paused in August and September ($664 million net Q3) [28, 35]. FY2026 adjusted expense guidance rose to ~$108.6 billion ahead of a 5.5% 2028 G-SIB cliff and ~6% Basel III CET1 lift [28, 32]. Meanwhile, ~$24 billion in Apple Card commitments ($106.7 billion unfunded lines), $449.1 billion in NBFI/SPE loans, and a 2027 CFO handoff from Jeremy Barnum to Bregje de Best require tight oversight [28, 29, 30].

Dual Verdict & Anti-Hedging Math: Business quality keeps its COMPOUNDER_PASS rating (kpi_health: PASS). Yet at the November 20, 2026 close of $310.68, we downgrade new capital to REJECTED (TIER_0: TREND, VALUATION) [34]. Shares trade at 13.03x TTM P/E, 2.76x stated Q3 TBVPS ($112.64), and 2.95x HTM-adjusted TBV ($105.26) [20, 28]. The stock plunged 10.31% over five sessions on 1.73x distribution volume into Stage 4 (CAP_REJECTED) [34]. It broke the 50-day SMA ($337.35), 30-week SMA ($334.16), 200-day SMA ($325.20), and prior $322.51 stop during a market Downtrend [34]. Enforcing our Gordon Growth identity (18.5% ROTCE, 9.5% CoE, 3.5% g = 2.50x P/TBV) sets 12-month Base fair value at $302.75 on $121.10 forward TBV (-2.55% vs. CMP) and $284.30 on $113.72 HTM-adjusted TBV (-8.49%). Because 2.76x current TBV still prices 20.06% perpetual ROTCE and reclaiming $334.16–$337.35 over a $315.27 Pivot S2 stop yields negative asymmetry (< 0:1 to $302.75), zero shares are held (NOT_HELD) and we keep 100% of our $2,540.35 US cash in reserve [34].

web_blocks.takeaway: JPMorgan Chase retains COMPOUNDER_PASS business quality, yet its Stage 4 breakdown ($310.68) and reconciled 2.50x Base value ($302.75 stated / $284.30 HTM-adjusted) dictate REJECTED (TIER_0) and 100% CASH.

web_blocks.html: Key Triggers & Watchpoints Ahead: Four checkpoints will decide whether JPMorgan exits the bench in 2027. First, watch for AOCI stabilization and quarterly share buybacks resuming above $5 billion [28, 35]. Second, track expense control against the ~$108.6 billion base under incoming CFO Bregje de Best [28, 29]. Third, monitor final U.S. Basel III capital rules and Apple Card credit reserves [28, 32]. Fourth, wait for BOTH a completed multi-week Stage 1 base AND either a high-volume Stage 2 reclaim above $334.16–$337.35 (with Base >$371) or a lower Stage 2 structure yielding ≥1.50:1 asymmetry anchored to HTM-adjusted TBVPS.

book_paragraphs: Every disciplined investment process exists to answer two separate questions without letting one contaminate the other: is this business built to compound across economic cycles, and are the current stock price and market trend paying you fairly for the risks you must shoulder today? On November 20, 2026, JPMorgan Chase & Co. forces us to give two sharply different answers to those two questions.

In our price-blind audit of Chapters 1 through 6, JPMorgan Chase cleanly retained its Compounder Pass rating. Across its Consumer, Commercial & Investment Bank, and $5.21 trillion Asset & Wealth Management engines, JPMorgan generated $157.36 billion in revenue and $52.95 billion in net income over the first nine months of 2026, sustaining a 20% reported ROTCE on 14.0% CET1 capital. Yet our refresh also uncovered real operational friction beneath those headline profits: -$19.82 billion in AOCI losses that nudged Q3 TBVPS down to $112.64, $25.84 billion in unrecorded HTM bond marks (-$7.38 per share after tax), an August–September share buyback pause, ~$108.6 billion in full-year expense guidance, a 5.5% 2028 G-SIB cliff, $449.1 billion of NBFI/SPE wholesale exposure, and CFO Jeremy Barnum's 2027 handoff to Bregje de Best.

When we lifted the veil on the November 20, 2026 market tape, the chart and the math delivered a clear stop sign. JPMorgan tumbled 10.31% in five sessions to $310.68 on 1.73x average volume, slicing beneath its 50-day, 30-week, and 200-day moving averages as well as our prior $322.51 stop to enter a confirmed Stage 4 breakdown during a broader S&P 500 Downtrend. Strictly applying the Gordon Growth identity (18.5% ROTCE, 9.5% CoE, 3.5% g = 2.50x P/TBV) yields a Base Case fair value of $302.75 stated ($284.30 HTM-adjusted), flanked by a $398.00 Bull Case ($374.84 HTM-adjusted) and a 2.00x Bear Case of $233.00 stated ($218.24 HTM-adjusted).

Here is why our anti-hedging rule demands an unhedged REJECTED (TIER_0) verdict rather than a lukewarm Wait for Support: exiting Stage 4 cleanly requires JPMorgan to reclaim its $334.16–$337.35 moving-average ceiling above a real $7.92-ATR structural stop at Pivot S2 ($315.27), yet our reconciled $302.75 stated ($284.30 HTM-adjusted) Base fair value already sits below both the current price and that reclaim band—leaving negative reward-to-risk (< 0:1). Because we hold zero shares (NOT_HELD), we stay 100% in cash, protect our portfolio during a Downtrend, and walk through the full evidence across the chapters ahead.

Whether you read this monograph for long-term banking education or immediate portfolio execution, keep one distinction clear from page one: a Compounder Pass business can still be a Rejected stock when its weekly trend breaks into Stage 4 and its Gordon Growth fair value sits below the reclaim threshold. With zero shares held and 100% of our marginal US cash parked safely in reserve, we can study JPMorgan Chase objectively and wait for the market to offer a true Stage 2 margin of safety.
